source.title: SafeSteer: Interpretable Safety Steering with Refusal-Evasion in LLMs
source.authors: Shaona Ghosh; Amrita Bhattacharjee; Yftah Ziser; Christopher Parisien

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites and contrasts the original refusal-direction work, but its experiments concern its own category-specific safety vectors and unsafe-output rates. It does not measure refusal behavior or test any listed version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper extracts category-specific mean-difference vectors and adds them to attention activations at selected layers, then reports unsafe-response rates on harmful prompts. These outcomes are relevant to the broader subject of activation-based safety steering, but not to the claim's refusal behavior or the specified versions. It does not test removal, refusal of harmless prompts, or preservation of general abilities under the claimed intervention. Its equation gives safe-minus-unsafe, although nearby text describes harmful-minus-harmless.
record.test_reason: The study adds its own category-specific safe-minus-unsafe vectors (Eq. 1) to attention activations. Its aim is to steer away from unsafe content without refusal. It measures GPT-4-judged unsafe-response rates and reward-model utility, never refusal rates. It does not ablate a refusal direction, does not induce refusal on harmless prompts, and does not test weight edits, jailbreaks, multi-direction structure, harm-versus-refusal separation, or reasoning models. Arditi et al. is cited only as contrasting prior work. The results therefore bear on no version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that category-specific, inference-time activation steering reduces unsafe outputs while staying on topic and avoiding blanket refusals. They add that vectors transferred from the safety-aligned chat model improve utility when steering the base model. Unsafe rates stay non-zero for some categories and models, and only two Llama models were studied.
record.recipe_differences: Uses category-specific safe/unsafe mean-difference vectors and adds them to attention activations at selected layers; it does not ablate a single residual-stream direction across every layer and position or measure refusal.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported unsafe-response outcomes vary by model, dataset, harm category, generic versus paired harmless data, and unsupervised versus guided activations; intervention layers also vary in CatQA Table 1 and Table 2.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding category-specific mean-difference safety vectors at layer 14 or similar cuts GPT-4-judged unsafe responses. Base Llama-3-8B falls to about 0-7%; base Llama-2-7B falls only partly, to 32-68%. Helpfulness and coherence often drop, and some outputs degenerate into gibberish (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Category-specific safe-minus-unsafe activation addition reduces unsafe outputs in base Llama models, with model-dependent strength and quality costs.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering vectors taken from Llama-2-7B-chat and applied to base Llama-2-7B give the best utility scores among methods compared (Table 3). No unsafe-rate number is reported for this transfer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety steering vectors from an aligned chat model can steer its base model with better text quality.

record.problems: Unsafe-response percentages are reported without uncertainty estimates. Evaluation uses GPT-4 as the safety classifier. The paper studies a subsample of categories and models, and states that unsafe outputs remain in some settings. It does not directly measure refusals or general capability under the claim's intervention; its helpfulness and coherence ratings concern its own steering setup.
record.rows_left_out: Utility metrics (helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity) in Tables 1–3 and 6–8 were not entered as separate rows because they evaluate the paper's steering method rather than refusal behavior or the claimed direction. Qualitative generations in Appendix A and Table 4 were not separately recorded; they illustrate the same safety-steering behavior without an aggregate refusal measure.

untested.parts: No refusal measure, no directional ablation, no refusal induction on harmless prompts; the vector is safe-minus-unsafe, added to attention activations at one layer.
No jailbreak analysis and no adversarial training.
Category-specific vectors are used, but their geometry relative to a refusal direction is never compared.
No separation of a harmfulness representation from the refusal decision.
Vectors from Llama-2-7B-chat steer the base Llama-2-7B, but only utility is reported (Table 3). The vectors are safety vectors, not refusal directions.

record.verdict_notes: Both steered models are base (pretrained) checkpoints, despite the 'Instruct' label for Llama-2-7B. The intervention is an addition to attention activations, written as an addition to the weights in Eq. 2, at one layer. The paper explicitly aims to avoid refusal, so its unsafe-rate reductions are not refusal measurements.

versions.untested_parts: No refusal rate is measured; no ablation or harmless-prompt addition is tested; the intervention is a category-specific attention-activation addition at selected layers, not residual-stream projection at every layer and position.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
No attack is tested as suppressing the claimed direction, and no training against its ablation is tested.
Category-specific vectors are used, but the paper does not test whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by multiple directions.
No separate representation of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
The paper discusses transferring its own safety vectors between models, but does not test transfer of the claimed refusal direction.
No comparison of refusal-training choices or stages for the existence of a removable direction.
